dossier.claim: Names acquire spelling errors, a first-name reassurance becomes surname address, and several exchanges lose or alter the particular form of address under discussion. These are distinct local problems rather than a rule that every Japanese name or title must remain in English.
dossier.sourcePattern: The examples name Sakura as the woman reacting, recall when Rin began using Shirou’s first name, address Saber directly, and use familiar or intimate names as part of the scene. Other passages require consistent spelling of an established name.
dossier.englishEffect: Toshaka and llyasviel disrupt established spellings. Rin calls him Emiya where the Japanese says Shirou; Illya’s distorted reply substitutes lady for big sister. Sakura’s blush is assigned to Tohsaka, and the timing of Rin’s first-name usage changes, while a question to Saber becomes a question about her. Illya’s switch from Shirou to big brother during her ownership demand becomes another use of his name.
dossier.limits: English can omit an unambiguous vocative, use you instead of a second-person name, and adapt a pronunciation joke to English name order. Suffixes need not be copied mechanically. The Saber-chan banter is a defensible adaptation of sudden familiarity and is excluded. The preserved brother farewell and Taiga’s explicitly explained surname switch limit any general claim of systematic address loss.
dossier.diagnostic: 30 findings in this category; 8 cited passages.
